title: Why video game characters say such ridiculous things (Kotaku; Dansky, Anderson, Dahlen, Hocking quoted)
rule: A bark is feedback about game state, so it carries one piece of information and is clear and unobtrusive; cleverness makes it less useful. Combining facts multiplies the variants you must write.
example: Dansky: "Ideally, each bark should convey one piece of information." ("We're flanking", "Grenade", "I've been hit"). Anderson: "Getting too 'clever' or flavourful can actually make the barks less useful." Hocking: "Game dialogue is a form of feedback."
game: Splinter Cell: Conviction; Far Cry 2; Mark of the Ninja

title: Why video game characters say such ridiculous things (Kotaku)
rule: Write for the Nth hearing: frequency makes a line memorable beyond intent, a small pool cycles fast, and a distinctive line is the first to grate. Late in production the good variants are used up, so budget pool depth early. Play-test each bark in its trigger context, since lines fine in isolation fail in play.
example: Dansky: "It's not only what is said, but also how often they're said." Dansky on a line heard repeatedly in one level: "is going to be a little more memorable than perhaps it was intended to be." Anderson: a Mark of the Ninja guard said "Guess I'm just imagining things" after the player broke a light, i.e. triggered by the very sound that proved otherwise. Cautionary cases: Conviction's "Fisher!" lines, Arkham City's overused "Bitch" barks.
game: Splinter Cell: Conviction; Batman: Arkham City; Mark of the Ninja

title: Dialogue barks timing and cooldown best practices (PulseGeek)
rule: Gate barks by cooldown per category (urgent short, ambient long), remember the last few lines per speaker, and fire only when the trigger adds new information or emotion. Cooldown should scale with line length. Figures are one site's recommendations, not studio-measured.
example: "try 1.0-2.0 seconds for damage confirmations"; "5-10 seconds for enemy spotted"; "12-20 seconds for ambient remarks"; "25-40 seconds for lore-friendly flavor during traversal"; repeat memory "the last 3-5 bark IDs per speaker". No variation-count target given.

title: Conversation (Emily Short)
rule: A line must not assume an order: gate on what the conversation has established, not on what the player happened to do first. Mark used lines so they are not repeated, but keep reusable answers re-askable, and ensure a really important question can never become impossible to ask in a context. Keep player menus to a few options (three to six).
example: "Quips can be tagged to indicate that they could follow only immediately after other quips." ("Where were you that night?" only after "I was at the docks.") "It takes some work, though, to make sure that really important questions never become entirely impossible to ask." Quip tree upside: "Dialogue flows, since the player is never confronted with the option" to ask out of sequence. Forever Always "lets the player see what he is going to say before he says it."

title: Analysis: Conversation Design In Games (Game Developer, after Short)
rule: Hub-and-spokes allows exploration but causes repetition and an implausibly patient NPC. Plan what happens to a used line: remove it, leave it, write an alternate repeat line, or offer a summary line (information-heavy games favour recall, relationship games favour non-repetition). Make a real choice by forcing the next line to follow the question immediately. Give NPCs initiative so they change subject when a topic ends.
example: "The advantage of a tree-based structure is that it's (relatively) easy to code, understand, and debug." "A pushy NPC might obsess or nag about a single topic." Non-modal conversation can "elevate NPCs from the status of objects to the status of fellow-participants in the game world."

title: Tom Francis on dialogue wheels (Pentadact)
rule: If the spoken line would be the same whichever option is picked, the option is a lie; cut it. Spoken line must match the stated attitude.
example: "If you can't give me the option, don't give me the option." He can tell before or after selecting that his character would have said the same thing; filler choices make developers "seem lazy." Good wheels are "so good I have to go away and make a cup of coffee before deciding." (Screenshots not described in text.)

title: Drew Karpyshyn interview (GameBanshee), via search snippet only
rule: Mass Effect paraphrased the wheel because the player's line is fully voiced: reading a full option then hearing it would feel like the line was delivered twice. Cost: the wheel text can mislead about the spoken line. Laidlaw (snippet): paraphrase does not give away exact wording or how the sentiment will be acted.

title: Game dialogue from hell: Afterparty's approach to player freedom (Game Informer)
rule: Fetched article is thin (says only the game lets you interrupt). Secondary search snippets, not verified at source: Oxenfree shows 2-3 bubble options over the speaker's head while the player keeps walking; options can be taken at any time, so waiting, interrupting and staying silent are all choices; Krankel: silence is itself a reaction. Reviewers noted accidental interruptions.
example: Snippet-level, paraphrased by the search tool: "how you can interrupt people, how not saying something is a choice, how to write for three dialogue choices".

title: Notes on Jon Ingold's AdventureX 2018 dialogue talk (Robert Yang, a summary with his interpretation)
rule: Offer three options that differ in attitude toward the conflict: accept (cooperate, answer), reject (attack), deflect (change the subject without breaking tone). Two options read as a false binary, four lack focus; avoid context-free filler like 'What do you think?'. The scene must do dramatic work, and branching structure is itself characterisation.
example: Rachel: "I'm Rachel." Accept: "Deckard." Reject: "I'm here to see Tyrell." (Rachel: "He's a busy man.") Deflect: "What do you do here, Rachel?" (Rachel: "I'm Tyrell's niece.") Ingold: "Branching is action, action is character, character is drama." Critique of an Assassin's Creed Odyssey scene: "It's not doing any dramatic work."
game: Assassin's Creed Odyssey (critique); Blade Runner (film model)

title: Same (Ingold via Yang)
rule: Use a loop while the conversation circles at the same intensity and leave it when stakes escalate; give a trapdoor to skip ahead. Loops slow the scene, trapdoors speed it. Sending the player back to the loop start punishes a choice and can show NPC power.
example: Choosing "I'm here to see Tyrell" skips the small talk; attacking Rachel's competency sends the player back to the start of the loop.

title: Developer shows how to write good game dialogue using Blade Runner (Kotaku, on Ingold)
rule: Fix the subtext as the structure and let the surface wording vary by player choice; if the meaningful interaction is in the subtext, the literal text matters less. Avoid a 'click on all the dialogue' design.
example: Ingold: "We assign the subtext as a fixed structure that we are not going to give up."

title: Writing dialogues for the Clean Spear tavern (Roadwarden devlog)
rule: In a text-only game, tag each option with an attitude that is a mask the player wears; paired near-identical options express character, not optimal play; attitude can rewrite the option text itself. Effects on the NPC stay hidden (no friendship meters).
example: Attitudes: Friendly, Playful, Distanced, Intimidating, Vulnerable. Pair: "It's easy to learn how to do it, but it's tiring." / "Quite hard, honestly. Not anyone can handle a palfrey." Intimidating version: "Shut up and answer my questions. I'm in a hurry."

title: Dialogue choices (Choice of Games forum)
rule: Tone-only labels ([Warmly]/[Coolly]) can feel like a wall; posters prefer the spoken line carrying the tone, or intonation implied in a narrated clause, mixed by situation. Forum opinion, small sample.
example: Original poster: tone-only choices "felt a little like a wall"; 13ventrm: "perhaps the intonation can be implied."

title: Neverwinter Nights community dialogue guide, via search snippet only
rule: Community norms for unvoiced text: NPC monologues of about 3-5 lines of roughly 25 words each, with the player able to interrupt or change subject; VN/RPG Maker advice of one idea or emotion per textbox; a mobile writing test capping a line at 100 characters. Not measured; the VN source page returned 403.

title: Firewatch (Edge 2015 interview), via search snippet only
rule: Silence is a valid reply and the script tracks what the player has told the other character. A timed-choice claim came from an unverified fan page and is not supported.
example: Vanaman (snippet): "The script is about 1000 printed pages, thousands of lines".

title: Kentucky Route Zero (Steam thread reproducing an Elliott interview; Haywire column), via search snippet
rule: Choices that reveal temperament (guarded or curious around a stranger) with no right or wrong answer, framed like a play read from a distance; lines can be cut up at word level because there are no recorded actors. Secondhand, check the original.

title: Use of LLMs in custom interactive fiction engines (intfiction), via search snippet only
rule: Commenters: LLMs repeat stock phrasing and a written-language register in speech; plausible use is short varied background one-liners, not main dialogue. Emily Short (per snippet): freedom to say anything to an NPC can put players off because they do not know what to do. A blog (hey.paris, snippet) argues a fixed line budget forces each authored line to work harder and free generation removes that pressure. All opinion.

title: Null results
rule: No usable developer source for companion banter writing (BioWare, Mass Effect, Last of Us); Kasavin's bark selection logic is behind a GDC login; Darkest Dungeon narrator writing method not found (only a player complaint that 'Mortality clarified in an instant' repeats in combat); no Avellone source retrieved. Modders report Baldur's Gate II EE tries a random party banter every 10 minutes at 10% chance (forum, unverified).
